label: Why analog automation lags digital
lesson:
# Why analog automation lags digital

Digital implementation runs from RTL to GDS with little human intervention. Analog design still relies on experts who size transistors by hand, draw matched layouts and iterate with SPICE. For a tool designer, the reasons are not historical accident: they come from what analog circuits compute, how their quality is measured and how expensive it is to evaluate a candidate. Understanding the gap tells you which automation problems are tractable now and which are still research.

## No abstraction that hides the devices

Digital automation rests on a ladder of abstractions. Boolean logic hides voltages, standard cells hide transistors, and a Liberty table hides a cell's internals behind slew and load. Each gate restores its output to a clean logic level, so small errors in one stage do not propagate, and stages can be designed and checked independently. Analog circuits have no such ladder. An amplifier's gain, bandwidth, noise and offset depend continuously on every width, length and bias current, and on the parasitics of the wires connecting them. There is no small library of context-free building blocks: a current mirror behaves differently depending on its output voltage, its load and its layout. That is why analog synthesis cannot reduce to choosing and connecting cells, and why each block is in practice designed for its context.

## Many specs, expensive evaluation

A digital block's quality reduces to a few scalars: worst slack, power, area. An analog block is judged on a vector of interacting specifications: DC gain, gain-bandwidth product, phase margin, slew rate, noise, offset, output swing, power, often across a dozen PVT corners and under mismatch. Improving one usually costs another, so sizing is constrained multi-objective optimization. Each candidate is evaluated by a nonlinear SPICE simulation. One run takes seconds to minutes, but corners times Monte Carlo samples times optimizer iterations multiplies it: 50 corners and 200 samples is 10,000 simulations for one candidate. The design space is also hostile: performance is nonconvex in the sizes, devices can leave saturation abruptly, and feasible regions are thin. An optimizer can afford only thousands of evaluations in a space where naive search would need millions.

## Where automation works today

The mature parts of the analog flow are verification engines: SPICE simulation (ngspice, Xyce and commercial simulators), corner and Monte Carlo analysis, DRC, LVS and parasitic extraction. Synthesis-like tasks are partially automated. Sizing is helped by gm/Id lookup tables, equation-based optimizers and simulation-in-the-loop methods such as Bayesian optimization. Layout is helped by constraint-driven generators such as MAGICAL and ALIGN, which recognize matched structures and place them symmetrically. Topology selection and specification remain human decisions. The most automatable problems share a property: the topology is fixed and the targets are known, as in re-sizing across corners or porting a block to a new process. A tool designer should expect value from automating search and verification inside a designer's intent, not from replacing that intent.

## Going deeper

Gielen and Rutenbar, "Computer-aided design of analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 2000); Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2017), chapter 1.

problems.q:
Digital synthesis can map any Boolean function onto a fixed library of characterized cells. What is the main reason analog design has no equivalent abstraction?

A) Analog circuits cannot be described by netlists

B) Analog circuits use more transistors than digital ones

C) Analog performance depends continuously on device sizes, bias and parasitics, so there is no small set of reusable cells with context-free behaviour

D) SPICE is too inaccurate to characterize analog cells
problems.a: Analog performance depends continuously on device sizes, bias and parasitics, so there is no small set of reusable cells with context-free behaviour
problems.e: A standard cell behaves the same anywhere once its slew and load are known. An analog block's gain, bandwidth and offset shift with every size, bias and parasitic, so behaviour cannot be abstracted into a fixed library.

problems.q:
Why does an analog layout change often force a re-simulation, while a digital layout change is usually checked by fast static timing?

A) Parasitics, matching and coupling change analog performance in ways no fast static check captures

B) Analog layouts have no design rules

C) Analog layouts are always hand-drawn, so no extraction exists

D) Static timing analysis is illegal for analog nets
problems.a: Parasitics, matching and coupling change analog performance in ways no fast static check captures
problems.e: Small parasitic capacitances move poles and mismatch shifts offsets; only a post-layout simulation of the extracted netlist shows the effect.

B) Analog circuits use more transistors than digital ones

D) Analog performance depends continuously on device sizes, bias and parasitics, so there is no small set of reusable cells with context-free behaviour
problems.a: Analog performance depends continuously on device sizes, bias and parasitics, so there is no small set of reusable cells with context-free behaviour
problems.e: A standard cell behaves the same anywhere once its slew and load are known. An analog block's gain, bandwidth and offset shift with every size, bias and parasitic, so behaviour cannot be abstracted into a fixed library.

problems.q:
A team wants to automate op-amp sizing. Which formulation captures the problem correctly?

A) Choose the topology that has the most citations

B) Choose widths, lengths, bias currents and compensation to minimize power or area subject to every spec holding at every PVT corner

C) Maximize gain with no other constraints

D) Minimize the number of transistors
problems.a: Choose widths, lengths, bias currents and compensation to minimize power or area subject to every spec holding at every PVT corner
problems.e: Sizing is constrained optimization over continuous device parameters with performance specs as constraints, evaluated robustly across corners.

problems.q:
An analog sizing tool must call SPICE to evaluate each candidate. What makes this the central cost of analog automation?

A) SPICE needs a license per transistor

B) Each evaluation is a nonlinear simulation, often repeated across corners and Monte Carlo samples, so the optimizer can afford only thousands of evaluations

C) SPICE cannot run in batch mode

D) SPICE results are random, so each point needs a million repeats
problems.a: Each evaluation is a nonlinear simulation, often repeated across corners and Monte Carlo samples, so the optimizer can afford only thousands of evaluations
problems.e: A single transient or AC run is cheap, but corners times samples times iterations multiplies it into the main budget an optimizer must respect.

problems.q:
A team wants to automate op-amp sizing. Which formulation captures the problem correctly?

A) Minimize the number of transistors

B) Choose widths, lengths, bias currents and compensation to minimize power or area subject to every spec holding at every PVT corner

C) Choose the topology that has the most citations

D) Maximize gain with no other constraints
problems.a: Choose widths, lengths, bias currents and compensation to minimize power or area subject to every spec holding at every PVT corner
problems.e: Sizing is constrained optimization over continuous device parameters with performance specs as constraints, evaluated robustly across corners.

problems.q:
Where is analog automation most likely to deliver value first in a company that already has expert designers?

A) Inventing new converter architectures

B) Removing the need for silicon validation

C) Porting existing blocks to a new process and re-centring them across corners, where specs and topology are already known

D) Replacing SPICE as the reference
problems.a: Porting existing blocks to a new process and re-centring them across corners, where specs and topology are already known
problems.e: Migration and re-sizing have a fixed topology and clear targets, so search and verification can be automated while designers keep the creative decisions.

problems.q:
Which part of analog design has been automated most successfully in production flows?

A) Specification writing

B) Choosing the fabrication process

C) Topology invention for new architectures

D) Simulation, corner and Monte Carlo verification, and rule-based checks such as DRC and LVS
problems.a: Simulation, corner and Monte Carlo verification, and rule-based checks such as DRC and LVS
problems.e: Verification engines are mature. Synthesis-style tasks such as topology selection and full sizing remain largely designer-driven, with automation assisting.

problems.q:
A designer sizes amplifiers with gm/Id lookup tables generated from the foundry models. What gap does this close?

A) It automates layout

B) It replaces inaccurate hand equations with simulated device data while keeping a fast, designer-guided procedure

C) It removes the need for any simulation

D) It eliminates process variation
problems.a: It replaces inaccurate hand equations with simulated device data while keeping a fast, designer-guided procedure
problems.e: Lookup tables carry real short-channel behaviour into hand design, so first-pass sizing lands close to simulation without a full optimizer loop.

label: The MOSFET small-signal model
lesson:
# The MOSFET small-signal model

Every analog hand calculation and every AC simulation starts by linearizing the transistors around their DC operating point. The small-signal model replaces a saturated MOSFET by a transconductance $g_m$, an output resistance $r_o$ and capacitances. A simulator computes these from the compact model at the operating point; a designer estimates them from the square law. Both views matter to a tool designer: the first is what AC analysis does, the second is what sizing equations assume.

## Linearizing around the operating point

In saturation the drain current is a nonlinear function $I_D(V_{GS}, V_{DS})$. For small signals around a bias point, a first-order Taylor expansion gives $i_d = g_m v_{gs} + g_{ds} v_{ds}$, with $g_m = \partial I_D/\partial V_{GS}$ and $g_{ds} = 1/r_o = \partial I_D/\partial V_{DS}$. The circuit becomes a voltage-controlled current source $g_m v_{gs}$ in parallel with $r_o$, plus gate capacitances $C_{gs}$, $C_{gd}$ and junction capacitances. This is exactly what an AC analysis does: it solves the DC operating point, evaluates the Jacobian of the device model there and solves a linear complex system at each frequency. The model is valid only while signals are small enough that the curvature of $I_D$ does not matter, typically a few millivolts at the gate.

## Square-law estimates of gm and ro

In the long-channel square law, $I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)V_{OV}^2$ with overdrive $V_{OV} = V_{GS} - V_T$. Differentiating gives three equivalent forms: $g_m = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)V_{OV} = 2I_D/V_{OV} = \sqrt{2\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$. Channel-length modulation adds a factor $(1+\lambda V_{DS})$, so $r_o \approx 1/(\lambda I_D)$. For $I_D = 100\ \mu$A at $V_{OV} = 0.2$ V, $g_m = 2 \cdot 100/0.2 = 1000\ \mu$S, or 1 mS. With $\lambda = 0.1\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$, $r_o = 1/(0.1 \cdot 10^{-4}) = 100$ kilohms. Note the scaling: at fixed current, $g_m$ grows only as the square root of $W/L$, while at fixed overdrive it grows linearly with current.

## Where the square law fails

Modern devices are not long-channel. Velocity saturation makes $I_D$ closer to linear in $V_{OV}$ at high overdrive, so $g_m$ saturates. In weak inversion the current is exponential in $V_{GS}$ and $g_m = I_D/(nU_T)$, larger than $2I_D/V_{OV}$ would predict. Output resistance depends on drain-induced barrier lowering and is a strong function of channel length, not a single $\lambda$. A compact model such as BSIM captures all of this, and the simulator's small-signal parameters come from it. For a tool designer the consequence is direct: an optimizer built on square-law equations finds the optimum of the wrong function. That is the motivation for the gm/Id methodology and lookup tables, which take $g_m$, $r_o$ and capacitances from simulated device data instead of from a formula.

## Going deeper

Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2017), chapters 2 and 3; Tsividis and McAndrew, "Operation and Modeling of the MOS Transistor" (3rd ed., 2011).

problems.q: An NMOS transistor in saturation carries $I_D = 190\ \mu$A at an overdrive voltage $V_{OV} = 0.11$ V. Using the square-law model, what is its transconductance $g_m$ in microsiemens? Round to the nearest integer.
problems.e: In the square law $I_D = \frac{k}{2}V_{OV}^2$, so $g_m = \partial I_D/\partial V_{GS} = kV_{OV} = 2I_D/V_{OV} = 2 \cdot 190 / 0.11 = 3455\ \mu$S.

problems.q: An NMOS transistor in saturation carries $I_D = 120\ \mu$A at an overdrive voltage $V_{OV} = 0.15$ V. Using the square-law model, what is its transconductance $g_m$ in microsiemens? Round to the nearest integer.
problems.e: In the square law $I_D = \frac{k}{2}V_{OV}^2$, so $g_m = \partial I_D/\partial V_{GS} = kV_{OV} = 2I_D/V_{OV} = 2 \cdot 120 / 0.15 = 1600\ \mu$S.

problems.q: An NMOS transistor in saturation carries $I_D = 210\ \mu$A at an overdrive voltage $V_{OV} = 0.38$ V. Using the square-law model, what is its transconductance $g_m$ in microsiemens? Round to the nearest integer.
problems.e: In the square law $I_D = \frac{k}{2}V_{OV}^2$, so $g_m = \partial I_D/\partial V_{GS} = kV_{OV} = 2I_D/V_{OV} = 2 \cdot 210 / 0.38 = 1105\ \mu$S.

problems.q: A saturated MOSFET has channel-length modulation $\lambda = 0.08\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ and carries $I_D = 190\ \mu$A. What is its small-signal output resistance $r_o$ in kilohms? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D) = 1/(0.08 \cdot 190 \times 10^{-6}) = 65.8$ kilohms.

problems.q: A saturated MOSFET has channel-length modulation $\lambda = 0.11\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ and carries $I_D = 450\ \mu$A. What is its small-signal output resistance $r_o$ in kilohms? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D) = 1/(0.11 \cdot 450 \times 10^{-6}) = 20.2$ kilohms.

problems.q: A saturated MOSFET has channel-length modulation $\lambda = 0.13\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ and carries $I_D = 420\ \mu$A. What is its small-signal output resistance $r_o$ in kilohms? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D) = 1/(0.13 \cdot 420 \times 10^{-6}) = 18.3$ kilohms.

problems.q: An NMOS device has $\mu_n C_{ox} = 200\ \mu\mathrm{A/V}^2$ and $W/L = 14$, biased in saturation at $I_D = 40\ \mu$A. Using $g_m = \sqrt{2\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$, what is $g_m$ in microsiemens? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m = \sqrt{2 \cdot 200 \cdot 14 \cdot 40} = 473.3\ \mu$S. Doubling $W/L$ at fixed current raises $g_m$ only by $\sqrt{2}$.

problems.q: An NMOS device has $\mu_n C_{ox} = 210\ \mu\mathrm{A/V}^2$ and $W/L = 25$, biased in saturation at $I_D = 180\ \mu$A. Using $g_m = \sqrt{2\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$, what is $g_m$ in microsiemens? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m = \sqrt{2 \cdot 210 \cdot 25 \cdot 180} = 1374.8\ \mu$S. Doubling $W/L$ at fixed current raises $g_m$ only by $\sqrt{2}$.

problems.q: An NMOS device has $\mu_n C_{ox} = 110\ \mu\mathrm{A/V}^2$ and $W/L = 22$, biased in saturation at $I_D = 350\ \mu$A. Using $g_m = \sqrt{2\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$, what is $g_m$ in microsiemens? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m = \sqrt{2 \cdot 110 \cdot 22 \cdot 350} = 1301.5\ \mu$S. Doubling $W/L$ at fixed current raises $g_m$ only by $\sqrt{2}$.

label: Decibels in analog and RF design
prereqs: Transfer functions and the Laplace domain
lesson:
# Decibels in analog and RF design

Analog and RF specifications are written in decibels: gain in dB, noise figure in dB, phase noise in dBc/Hz, power in dBm, converter SNR in dB. Logarithmic units turn cascades of multiplications into sums and compress ratios spanning many orders of magnitude. Getting the factor of 10 versus 20 wrong is one of the most common errors in hand analysis and in tool scripts, so the conversions must be automatic.

## Power ratios and voltage ratios

A decibel measures a power ratio: $G_{dB} = 10\log_{10}(P_2/P_1)$. Power is proportional to voltage squared across the same impedance, so a voltage ratio uses $20\log_{10}(V_2/V_1)$. Both give the same number when the impedances are equal. A voltage gain of 1000 V/V is $20\log_{10}(1000) = 60$ dB; a power gain of 1000 is 30 dB. Useful anchors: a factor of 2 in power is 3.01 dB, a factor of 2 in voltage is 6.02 dB, and a factor of 10 in voltage is 20 dB. Op-amp gain, filter attenuation and S-parameter magnitudes are voltage-like quantities and use 20; noise power, signal power and noise factor use 10.

## Absolute levels in dBm

Appending a reference turns a ratio into an absolute level. dBm is power relative to 1 mW: $P_{dBm} = 10\log_{10}(P/1\ \mathrm{mW})$. So 1 mW is 0 dBm, 100 mW is 20 dBm and 1 microwatt is -30 dBm. Converting back, $P = 10^{P_{dBm}/10}$ mW: -17 dBm is $10^{-1.7} = 0.020$ mW. Related units appear constantly: dBc is power relative to the carrier (used for spurs and phase noise), dBV is voltage relative to 1 V, and dBFS is relative to a converter's full scale. A gain in dB added to a level in dBm gives a level in dBm; adding two levels in dBm is meaningless, because the powers must be summed in milliwatts first.

## Cascades add in dB

Because logarithms turn products into sums, the gain of a cascade is the sum of the stage gains in dB. A chain of a 12 dB stage, a stage of 7 V/V and a 3 dB attenuator has total gain $12 + 20\log_{10}7 - 3 = 12 + 16.90 - 3 = 25.90$ dB. Losses are negative gains. This is why RF link budgets, ADC signal chains and photonic loss budgets are written as columns of dB values. The subtlety is what does not add in dB: noise powers from independent sources, intercept points and noise factors in a cascade must be combined in linear units (the Friis and IIP3 cascade formulas), then converted back. A tool that stores everything in dB must convert at exactly those points.

## Going deeper

Lee, "The Design of CMOS Radio-Frequency Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2004), chapter 1; Pozar, "Microwave Engineering" (4th ed., 2012).

problems.q: An amplifier has a voltage gain of 5946 V/V. What is the gain in decibels? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Voltage ratios use $20\log_{10}$: $20\log_{10}(5946) = 75.48$ dB.

problems.q: A stage delivers 4562 times more power to its load than it draws from its source. What is its power gain in decibels? Round to 2 decimal places.
A stage delivers 2437 times more power to its load than it draws from its source. What is its power gain in decibels? Round to 2 decimal places.
A receiver input sees 5.5 dBm. What is this power in milliwatts? Round to 4 decimal places.
A receiver input sees -34 dBm. What is this power in milliwatts? Round to 4 decimal places.
A signal generator outputs 158.26 mW. What is this power in dBm? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: dBm is power relative to 1 mW: $10\log_{10}(158.26 / 1) = 21.99$ dBm.

problems.q: A chain has a 17.5 dB voltage-gain stage, then a stage with voltage gain 2 V/V, then a 2.5 dB attenuator. What is the total voltage gain in dB? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Convert the middle stage, $20\log_{10}(2) = 6.02$ dB, then add the cascade in dB: $17.5 + 6.02 - 2.5 = 21.02$ dB.

problems.q: A chain has a 22 dB voltage-gain stage, then a stage with voltage gain 38 V/V, then a 7.5 dB attenuator. What is the total voltage gain in dB? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Convert the middle stage, $20\log_{10}(38) = 31.6$ dB, then add the cascade in dB: $22 + 31.6 - 7.5 = 46.1$ dB.

problems.q: A chain has a 12 dB voltage-gain stage, then a stage with voltage gain 39 V/V, then a 9 dB attenuator. What is the total voltage gain in dB? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Convert the middle stage, $20\log_{10}(39) = 31.82$ dB, then add the cascade in dB: $12 + 31.82 - 9 = 34.82$ dB.

label: Intrinsic gain gm times ro
prereqs: Decibels in analog and RF design
lesson:
# Intrinsic gain gm times ro

The intrinsic gain $g_m r_o$ is the largest voltage gain a single transistor can deliver, reached when it drives an ideal current-source load. It sets how many stages or cascodes an amplifier needs, and it has collapsed with scaling: from several hundred in long-channel devices to tens or less in nanometre processes. Sizing tools treat it as a device figure of merit read from lookup tables.

## The best single-transistor gain

A common-source transistor with an ideal current-source load has output resistance $r_o$, so its gain is $-g_m r_o$. Any real load is in parallel with $r_o$ and can only lower the gain. That makes $A_i = g_m r_o$ an upper bound on what one device contributes. With $g_m = 1.5$ mS and $r_o = 80$ kilohms, $A_i = 120$ V/V, about 41.6 dB. Millisiemens times kilohms is dimensionless, a convenient unit pair for hand work. In a differential pair with a mirror load, or in the second stage of an op-amp, each stage's gain is a fraction of this bound, so an 80 dB op-amp needs roughly two stages of 40 dB each, or cascodes.

## The current cancels

Substituting square-law expressions, $g_m = 2I_D/V_{OV}$ and $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)$, gives $g_m r_o = 2/(\lambda V_{OV})$. The drain current cancels: intrinsic gain depends on the bias point (overdrive) and on channel length through $\lambda$, not on how much current flows. For $\lambda = 0.1\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ and $V_{OV} = 0.2$ V the gain is 100. In gm/Id terms, $g_m r_o = (g_m/I_D)(I_D r_o) = (g_m/I_D)V_A$, where $V_A = 1/\lambda$ is the Early voltage. A device at $g_m/I_D = 15\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ with $V_A = 6$ V has intrinsic gain 90, or 39.1 dB. Higher $g_m/I_D$ (lower overdrive) and longer channels both raise gain.

## Why scaling hurts and what designers do

Short-channel effects shrink the Early voltage: drain-induced barrier lowering lets the drain modulate the channel, so $r_o$ falls as $L$ shrinks. In advanced planar nodes a minimum-length device may have intrinsic gain of 10 or less; FinFETs recover some through better electrostatics, but long channels are still used for gain. Designers respond with longer $L$ for gain-critical devices (at the cost of capacitance and speed), cascodes that multiply output resistance by another $g_m r_o$, and gain-boosting loops. For a tool designer, intrinsic gain is a function of $L$ and $g_m/I_D$ that must come from simulated tables, because $\lambda$ is not a constant: it is bias- and length-dependent, and a single number in an optimizer's model will mislead it.

## Going deeper

Jespers and Murmann, "Systematic Design of Analog CMOS Circuits Using Pre-Computed Lookup Tables" (2017), chapter 2.

problems.q: A transistor has $g_m = 1.5$ mS and $r_o = 95$ kilohms. What is its intrinsic gain $g_m r_o$ in V/V? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Millisiemens times kilohms is dimensionless: $1.5 \cdot 95 = 142.5$ V/V.

problems.q: A transistor has $g_m = 0.4$ mS and $r_o = 182$ kilohms. What is its intrinsic gain $g_m r_o$ in V/V? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Millisiemens times kilohms is dimensionless: $0.4 \cdot 182 = 72.8$ V/V.

problems.q: A transistor has $g_m = 3.7$ mS and $r_o = 61$ kilohms. What is its intrinsic gain $g_m r_o$ in V/V? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Millisiemens times kilohms is dimensionless: $3.7 \cdot 61 = 225.7$ V/V.

problems.q: In the square-law model with channel-length modulation $\lambda = 0.26\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$, a device runs at $V_{OV} = 0.11$ V. What is its intrinsic gain in V/V? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m = 2I_D/V_{OV}$ and $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)$, so $g_m r_o = 2/(\lambda V_{OV}) = 2/(0.26 \cdot 0.11) = 69.9$. The current cancels.

problems.q: In the square-law model with channel-length modulation $\lambda = 0.15\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$, a device runs at $V_{OV} = 0.34$ V. What is its intrinsic gain in V/V? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m = 2I_D/V_{OV}$ and $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)$, so $g_m r_o = 2/(\lambda V_{OV}) = 2/(0.15 \cdot 0.34) = 39.2$. The current cancels.

problems.q: In the square-law model with channel-length modulation $\lambda = 0.12\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$, a device runs at $V_{OV} = 0.33$ V. What is its intrinsic gain in V/V? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m = 2I_D/V_{OV}$ and $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)$, so $g_m r_o = 2/(\lambda V_{OV}) = 2/(0.12 \cdot 0.33) = 50.5$. The current cancels.

problems.q: A device is biased at $g_m/I_D = 5\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ and has an Early voltage $V_A = 1/\lambda = 4.5$ V at its channel length. What is its intrinsic gain in dB? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m r_o = (g_m/I_D)(I_D r_o) = (g_m/I_D) V_A = 5 \cdot 4.5 = 22.5$ V/V, which is 27 dB.

problems.q: A device is biased at $g_m/I_D = 5\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ and has an Early voltage $V_A = 1/\lambda = 13$ V at its channel length. What is its intrinsic gain in dB? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m r_o = (g_m/I_D)(I_D r_o) = (g_m/I_D) V_A = 5 \cdot 13 = 65$ V/V, which is 36.3 dB.

problems.q: A device is biased at $g_m/I_D = 11\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ and has an Early voltage $V_A = 1/\lambda = 3$ V at its channel length. What is its intrinsic gain in dB? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $g_m r_o = (g_m/I_D)(I_D r_o) = (g_m/I_D) V_A = 11 \cdot 3 = 33$ V/V, which is 30.4 dB.

label: The gm/Id methodology
lesson:
# The gm/Id methodology

The gm/Id methodology sizes transistors by choosing their transconductance efficiency $g_m/I_D$ first. That one number sets the inversion level, and with it the trade-off between current, speed, gain and signal swing. It works from weak to strong inversion where the square law does not, and it maps naturally onto tables of simulated device data, which is why it underlies most modern hand sizing and many automated sizers.

## Transconductance efficiency

$g_m/I_D$ measures how much transconductance each unit of current buys, in $\mathrm{V}^{-1}$. Most analog specs ask for a transconductance: GBW sets $g_m$ of an input pair, noise sets $g_m$ of critical devices, a pole position sets $g_m$ of a driver. Given the required $g_m$ and a chosen $g_m/I_D$, the current follows immediately: $I_D = g_m/(g_m/I_D)$. A stage needing $g_m = 1$ mS at $g_m/I_D = 20\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ needs $I_D = 50\ \mu$A; at $g_m/I_D = 10$ it needs 100 microamperes. Power is current times supply, so $g_m/I_D$ is a direct power knob. The width then follows from the current density at that $g_m/I_D$, which is the job of a lookup table.

## Inversion level and its limits

$g_m/I_D$ is a monotone function of the inversion level. In strong inversion the square law gives $g_m/I_D = 2/V_{OV}$: $g_m/I_D = 10$ corresponds to $V_{OV} = 200$ mV. As the gate voltage drops toward threshold the device enters moderate and then weak inversion, where the current is exponential in $V_{GS}$ and $g_m/I_D$ approaches its ceiling $1/(nU_T)$, with $U_T = kT/q \approx 25.9$ mV at 300 K and slope factor $n$ around 1.2 to 1.5. For $n = 1.3$ the ceiling is about 29.7 per volt. Typical design values span 5 (strong inversion, fast, large swing) to about 25 (weak inversion, efficient, slow). Unlike the square law, the methodology stays valid across the whole range because it does not assume a current equation.

## The speed and efficiency trade-off

Efficiency is not free. At high $g_m/I_D$ the device is wide for its current, so its gate capacitance is large and its transit frequency $f_T \approx g_m/(2\pi C_{gg})$ falls. At low $g_m/I_D$ it is small and fast but burns current. A device at $g_m/I_D = 15$ with $I_D = 40\ \mu$A has $g_m = 600\ \mu$S; with $C_{gg} = 50$ fF, $f_T = 600/(2\pi \cdot 50) = 1.91$ GHz (microsiemens over femtofarads is $10^9$ per second). The product $(g_m/I_D) f_T$ peaks in moderate inversion, which is why many optimized designs sit there. A sizer that searches over $g_m/I_D$ and $L$ instead of $W$ and $V_{GS}$ works in variables that map directly onto these trade-offs and stay well-scaled across processes.

## Going deeper

label: Lookup-table design with gm/Id
lesson:
# Lookup-table design with gm/Id

Lookup-table design replaces device equations by tables generated once from SPICE sweeps of the foundry model. Indexed by $g_m/I_D$ and channel length, they give current density, intrinsic gain, transit frequency and capacitances. Sizing becomes table lookups and interpolation, accurate to the model, fast enough for scripts and optimizers, and portable to a new process by regenerating the tables.

## Current density sets the width

For a fixed channel length and bias conditions, the drain current scales linearly with width, so the useful quantity is the current density $I_D/W$. A table sweeps $V_{GS}$ on a unit-width device and records $g_m/I_D$, $I_D/W$, $g_m/g_{ds}$, $f_T$ and $C_{gg}/W$ at each point. Reindexing by $g_m/I_D$ gives rows such as: at $g_m/I_D = 14$, $I_D/W = 9.5\ \mu$A/$\mu$m and $g_m/g_{ds} = 32$. Once the required current is known, the width is a division: a device carrying 76 microamperes at that point needs $W = 76/9.5 = 8\ \mu$m. Because density depends on $L$ and $V_{DS}$, real tables are multi-dimensional, but the procedure is the same.

## Interpolating between rows

A design point rarely lands on a table row. Linear interpolation between neighbouring rows is the simplest estimate: for $g_m/I_D = 15$ between rows at 14 and 18 with densities 9.5 and 4.1, the fraction is $(15 - 14)/(18 - 14) = 0.25$ and the estimate is $9.5 + 0.25(4.1 - 9.5) = 8.15\ \mu$A/$\mu$m. Current density falls roughly exponentially with $g_m/I_D$ toward weak inversion, so interpolating $\log(I_D/W)$ is more accurate, and production scripts use splines over fine sweeps. The table resolution is a design decision: a coarse table is fast to generate but adds error that an optimizer will treat as real. This is ordinary numerical interpolation, with its error term, applied to device data.

## A complete sizing step

A lookup-table sizing step chains the pieces. A spec gives $g_m$; the designer chooses $g_m/I_D$ and $L$ from the trade-offs (gain from $g_m/g_{ds}$, speed from $f_T$); the current is $g_m/(g_m/I_D)$; the width is the current over the density. For $g_m = 600\ \mu$S at $g_m/I_D = 12$: $I_D = 50\ \mu$A, and with density 20 the width is 2.5 micrometres. The same row gives the intrinsic gain and capacitance without another simulation, so the stage's gain and poles can be predicted at once. A sizing script that does this for every device lands close to the simulated result on the first pass, which is why gm/Id tables are both a designer's tool and the inner model of several automated sizers and migration flows.

## Going deeper

Jespers and Murmann, "Systematic Design of Analog CMOS Circuits Using Pre-Computed Lookup Tables" (2017), chapters 2 to 4.

label: The common-source amplifier
lesson:
# The common-source amplifier

The common-source stage is the basic voltage amplifier: input at the gate, output at the drain, source at a fixed potential. Every op-amp gain stage is a variant of it. Its small-signal analysis introduces the three quantities a designer and a sizing tool track for every stage: gain, output resistance and the pole formed at the output node.

## Gain is transconductance times output resistance

Replace the transistor by its small-signal model. The input voltage produces a drain current $g_m v_{in}$, which flows into the parallel combination of the load and the transistor's own $r_o$. Writing KCL at the drain gives $v_{out} = -g_m (R_D \parallel r_o) v_{in}$. With $g_m = 2$ mS, $R_D = 20$ kilohms and $r_o = 100$ kilohms, $R_D \parallel r_o = 16.67$ kilohms and the gain is -33.3 V/V. The minus sign means inversion. Raising $R_D$ raises gain but also the DC drop across it, eating headroom, which is why integrated stages use current-source loads: their high small-signal resistance gives gain without a large DC drop, pushing the gain toward the intrinsic limit $g_m r_o$.

## Source degeneration

A resistor $R_S$ between source and ground feeds back the output current: the gate-source voltage becomes $v_{in} - i_d R_S$. Solving gives an effective transconductance $G_m = g_m/(1 + g_m R_S)$, and, ignoring $r_o$, a gain of $-G_m R_D = -g_m R_D/(1 + g_m R_S)$. For $g_m = 4$ mS, $R_S = 1$ kilohm and $R_D = 20$ kilohms, $G_m = 0.8$ mS and the gain is -16, down from -80 without degeneration. When $g_m R_S \gg 1$ the gain approaches $-R_D/R_S$, a ratio of resistors that matches well and varies little with process. That is the general bargain of negative feedback: less gain, more linearity and predictability.

## The output pole

The output node sees resistance $R_{out} = R_D \parallel r_o$ and the load capacitance $C_L$ plus device capacitances. Together they form a pole at $f_p = 1/(2\pi R_{out} C_L)$. With $R_{out} = 16.67$ kilohms and $C_L = 1$ pF the time constant is 16.67 ns (kilohms times picofarads is nanoseconds) and $f_p = 9.55$ MHz. The gain-bandwidth product $g_m R_{out} \cdot 1/(2\pi R_{out} C_L) = g_m/(2\pi C_L)$ does not depend on $R_{out}$: raising the load resistance trades bandwidth for gain one for one. The input also sees $C_{gd}$ multiplied by the gain (the Miller effect), which can create a second pole at the input. For a sizing tool, every high-impedance node is a pole to account for in stability.

## Going deeper

label: Current mirrors and cascodes
lesson:
# Current mirrors and cascodes

Current mirrors copy and scale bias currents across a chip and serve as active loads. Their accuracy and output resistance set bias precision, gain and power-supply rejection. Cascoding raises output resistance by a factor of one intrinsic gain. These are among the most frequently recognized structures in analog layout tools, which must match their devices.

## Copying current through equal gate voltage

A diode-connected transistor M1 carries a reference current and develops the $V_{GS}$ needed to sink it. A second transistor M2 with the same $V_{GS}$ and the same $V_T$ and $L$ carries a current scaled by the width ratio: $I_{OUT} = I_{REF}(W_2/L_2)/(W_1/L_1)$. A 2:5 width ratio copies 40 microamperes into 100. Ratios are built from identical unit fingers (two units and five units) rather than different widths, so that edge effects scale with the ratio and the devices can be interdigitated. Changing $L$ between devices is avoided, because short-channel effects make $L$ ratios inaccurate. The mirror's accuracy is then limited by $V_{DS}$ mismatch and by device mismatch.

## Channel-length modulation and copy error

Equal $V_{GS}$ does not give equal currents when $V_{DS}$ differs, because $I_D \propto 1 + \lambda V_{DS}$. The diode device sits at $V_{DS1} = V_{GS}$; the output device sits wherever the load puts it. So $I_{OUT} = I_{REF}(1+\lambda V_{DS2})/(1+\lambda V_{DS1})$. For $\lambda = 0.2\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$, $V_{GS} = 0.6$ V and $V_{DS2} = 1.2$ V the error is $1.24/1.12 = 1.107$, an 11% copy error. The same effect gives the mirror a finite output resistance $r_o$, which limits its use as a load. The cures are longer channels (smaller $\lambda$) and cascodes that hold $V_{DS2}$ close to $V_{DS1}$.

## The cascode multiplies output resistance

Stacking a common-gate device M2 on top of the current-source device M1 shields M1's drain from the output. A change $\Delta V$ at the output barely moves M1's drain, because M2 needs only a tiny gate-source change to absorb it. The small-signal result is $R_{out} \approx g_{m2} r_{o2} r_{o1}$: the cascode multiplies $r_{o1}$ by its own intrinsic gain. With $g_{m2} = 1$ mS and both $r_o = 50$ kilohms, $R_{out} \approx 50 \cdot 50$ kilohms $= 2.5$ megohms, 50 times the simple mirror. The cost is headroom: the output must stay above two saturation voltages. As supplies fall, that headroom becomes scarce, which is why low-voltage designs and migration flows must track stacked $V_{DS,sat}$ budgets explicitly.

## Going deeper

Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2017), chapter 5.

label: The differential pair
lesson:
# The differential pair

The differential pair is the input stage of nearly every op-amp, comparator and OTA. It amplifies the difference between two inputs and rejects their common part, which makes it robust to supply noise and interference. Its symmetry is the reason analog layout tools treat differential pairs as their most important matching constraint.

## Splitting the tail current

Two matched transistors share a source node fed by a tail current $I_{SS}$. With equal inputs each carries $I_{SS}/2$. A small differential input $v_{id}$ moves current from one side to the other: $\Delta i = g_m v_{id}/2$ in each device, where $g_m$ is the transconductance of one device at $I_{SS}/2$. In gm/Id terms, $g_{m1} = (g_m/I_D)(I_{SS}/2)$: a 200 microampere tail at $g_m/I_D = 15$ gives $g_{m1} = 1.5$ mS. A common-mode input moves both gates together; ideally the tail holds the total current fixed and nothing changes at the outputs. Finite tail impedance and mismatch let some common-mode signal through, which is what CMRR measures.

## The five-transistor OTA

Loading the pair with a current mirror converts the differential current into a single-ended output. The mirror copies one side's current change to the output node, where it adds to the other side's opposite change, so the full $g_{m1}v_{id}$ flows into the output resistance $r_{o2} \parallel r_{o4}$. The differential gain is $A_d = g_{m1}(r_{o2} \parallel r_{o4})$. With $g_{m1} = 0.5$ mS and both output resistances 200 kilohms, $A_d = 0.5 \cdot 100 = 50$ V/V. This stage is the first stage of the classic two-stage op-amp. The mirror's own pole at its gate node introduces a pole-zero doublet, usually at high enough frequency to ignore in first-order design.

## Large-signal range

The linear model holds only for small inputs. In the square law, one device carries the whole tail current once $|v_{id}| \ge \sqrt{2}\,V_{OV}$, where $V_{OV}$ is the balanced overdrive. A pair at $V_{OV} = 0.15$ V saturates beyond 212 mV of differential input. Lower overdrive (higher $g_m/I_D$) gives more $g_m$ per unit current but a narrower linear range, so input pairs of comparators and low-noise amplifiers sit at high $g_m/I_D$ while pairs that must handle large swings sit lower. Source degeneration widens the range at the cost of gain. A sizing tool that optimizes only small-signal specs can produce a pair that slews or distorts badly for realistic inputs; large-signal specs such as slew rate and linearity must appear in the formulation too.

## Going deeper

Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2017), chapter 4.

label: The two-stage op-amp
prereqs: Decibels in analog and RF design
lesson:
# The two-stage op-amp

The Miller-compensated two-stage op-amp is the canonical benchmark circuit of analog design automation: a differential input stage for gain and common-mode rejection, a common-source second stage for more gain and output swing, and a compensation capacitor for stability. Almost every sizing paper and tool demonstrates on it, so its gain, bandwidth and pole structure are the first things a tool designer should be able to compute.

## Gain of two cascaded stages

The first stage is a differential pair with mirror load, gain $A_1 = g_{m1}(r_{o2} \parallel r_{o4})$. The second is a common-source stage with a current-source load, gain $A_2 = g_{m6}(r_{o6} \parallel r_{o7})$. The DC open-loop gain is $A_0 = A_1 A_2$, and in dB the stage gains add. With $A_1 = 40$ and $A_2 = 50$, $A_0 = 2000$, which is 66 dB. Each stage contributes roughly half an intrinsic gain, so in a process with intrinsic gain around 50, two stages land between 60 and 70 dB. Higher gain needs cascoded stages, longer channels or a third stage, each with a cost in swing, speed or stability.

## Gain-bandwidth set by gm1 and Cc

With Miller compensation the compensation capacitor $C_c$ between the second stage's input and output dominates the frequency response. The first stage's output current $g_{m1}v_{id}$ flows into $C_c$, which behaves as an integrator near crossover, so the unity-gain frequency is $\mathrm{GBW} = g_{m1}/(2\pi C_c)$. With $g_{m1} = 300\ \mu$S and $C_c = 1$ pF, $\mathrm{GBW} = 47.7$ MHz (microsiemens over picofarads is $10^6$ per second). The second stage does not appear: as long as the non-dominant poles are far above GBW, the product of gain and bandwidth is fixed by these two quantities. That is why sizing procedures start from GBW and $C_c$ to set $g_{m1}$, then pick $g_m/I_D$ to set the input pair's current.

## The dominant pole

A single-pole response with DC gain $A_0$ and gain-bandwidth GBW has its dominant pole at $f_{p1} = \mathrm{GBW}/A_0$. For 80 dB ($A_0 = 10^4$) and 50 MHz, $f_{p1} = 5$ kHz. The pole sits at the first-stage output, where the Miller-multiplied capacitance $C_c(1 + A_2)$ meets the first stage's output resistance. That the dominant pole is so low, kilohertz for a megahertz amplifier, is what makes the op-amp useful: it trades open-loop bandwidth for a gain that feedback converts into accuracy. The remaining poles, from the output node and the mirror, must sit well above GBW for the loop to be stable, which is the subject of compensation and phase margin.

## Going deeper

Allen and Holberg, "CMOS Analog Circuit Design" (3rd ed., 2011), chapter 6; Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2017), chapter 10.

label: Miller compensation and pole splitting
lesson:
# Miller compensation and pole splitting

An uncompensated two-stage op-amp has two low-frequency poles close together and would oscillate in feedback. Miller compensation, a capacitor across the second stage, separates them: it pushes one pole down and the other up. It also creates a right-half-plane zero. These three locations, dominant pole, output pole and zero, are what sizing tools must place correctly.

## The Miller effect

A capacitor $C_c$ connected across an inverting stage of gain $-A_2$ draws current $C_c(1 + A_2)\,dv/dt$ from its input side, because the voltage across it changes $1 + A_2$ times as fast as the input. Seen from the input, it looks like a capacitance $C_c(1 + A_2)$ to ground. A 2 pF capacitor across a stage with gain 50 appears as 102 pF. Placed at the high-resistance output of the first stage, this large effective capacitance creates a very low pole, the dominant pole of the op-amp. The same effect is what makes the gate-drain capacitance of a common-source stage limit its input bandwidth; in compensation it is exploited deliberately.

## Pole splitting

Without $C_c$ the poles are $1/(R_1 C_1)$ and $1/(R_2 C_2)$ at the two stage outputs. With $C_c$, analysis of the two-node circuit gives approximately $p_1 \approx 1/(g_{m6}R_1 R_2 C_c)$ and $p_2 \approx g_{m6}C_c/(C_1 C_2 + C_c(C_1 + C_2))$. When $C_c$ and the load $C_2 = C_L$ dominate $C_1$, the second reduces to $p_2 \approx g_{m6}/C_L$. The dominant pole moves down and the output pole moves up: the poles split. For $g_{m6} = 2$ mS and $C_L = 2$ pF, $f_{p2} \approx 2000/(2\pi \cdot 2) = 159$ MHz. The physical picture: at high frequency $C_c$ shorts the second stage's gate to its drain, making it a diode-connected device whose low resistance $1/g_{m6}$ drives the load.

## The right-half-plane zero and its fix

$C_c$ also provides a feedforward path from the second stage's input to its output. At the frequency where the current through $C_c$ equals $g_{m6}v_{gs}$, the two cancel, giving a zero at $z = g_{m6}/C_c$ in the right half plane. It raises magnitude like a normal zero but lags phase like a pole, which erodes phase margin. With $g_{m6} = 2$ mS and $C_c = 1$ pF, $f_z = 318$ MHz. The standard fix is a nulling resistor $R_z$ in series with $C_c$, which moves the zero to $1/(C_c(1/g_{m6} - R_z))$. Choosing $R_z = 1/g_{m6}$, here 500 ohms, pushes the zero to infinity; a slightly larger $R_z$ moves it into the left half plane, where it can be placed on $p_2$ to cancel it.

## Going deeper

Gray, Hurst, Lewis and Meyer, "Analysis and Design of Analog Integrated Circuits" (5th ed., 2009), chapter 9; Allen and Holberg, "CMOS Analog Circuit Design" (3rd ed., 2011), chapter 6.

label: Stability and phase margin
lesson:
# Stability and phase margin

An amplifier in negative feedback is stable only if its loop gain loses enough phase before reaching unity magnitude. Phase margin measures that distance and predicts overshoot and ringing in the closed-loop step response. It is a hard spec in every op-amp sizing problem and the quantity most easily destroyed by layout parasitics, so a tool designer must be able to compute it from pole and zero positions.

## Phase margin from the loop gain

Feedback is unstable when the loop gain $T(j\omega)$ reaches -1: magnitude one with phase -180 degrees. Phase margin is $\mathrm{PM} = 180 + \angle T(j\omega_u)$, where $\omega_u$ is the unity-gain frequency. For left-half-plane poles the phase is a sum of arctangents: $\angle T = -\sum_i \arctan(\omega_u/p_i)$. Take poles at 0.01 MHz and 100 MHz with crossover at 50 MHz: the first contributes $\arctan(5000) \approx 89.99$ degrees, the second $\arctan(0.5) = 26.57$ degrees, so $\mathrm{PM} = 180 - 89.99 - 26.57 = 63.4$ degrees. The argument of each factor of the transfer function adds, so phase computation is just complex-argument arithmetic at one frequency.

## Zeros and the right-half plane

A left-half-plane zero at $z$ adds $+\arctan(\omega_u/z)$ of phase. A right-half-plane zero adds magnitude like a normal zero but subtracts $\arctan(\omega_u/z)$, like a pole. In a Miller op-amp the uncancelled zero at $g_{m6}/C_c$ is often only a few times GBW. With poles at 0.01 and 100 MHz, crossover at 50 MHz and a right-half-plane zero at 250 MHz, the zero costs $\arctan(0.2) = 11.3$ degrees and the margin falls from 63.4 to 52.1 degrees. This is why the nulling resistor matters, and why a sizing tool that ignores the zero overestimates phase margin. The rule generalizes: any element whose phase lags at crossover, pole or right-half-plane zero or delay, subtracts from the margin.

## Designing for a target margin

With a dominant pole far below crossover, it contributes almost exactly -90 degrees, so $\mathrm{PM} \approx 90 - \arctan(\mathrm{GBW}/f_{p2})$. Inverting gives the required non-dominant pole: $f_{p2} = \mathrm{GBW}/\tan(90 - \mathrm{PM})$. For 60 degrees, $f_{p2} = \mathrm{GBW}/\tan 30 = 1.73\,\mathrm{GBW}$; for 45 degrees, $f_{p2} = \mathrm{GBW}$. Many sizing procedures use $f_{p2} \ge 2.2\,\mathrm{GBW}$, which gives about 65.6 degrees. Since $f_{p2} \approx g_{m6}/(2\pi C_L)$ and $\mathrm{GBW} = g_{m1}/(2\pi C_c)$, the condition becomes $g_{m6}/C_L \ge 2.2\,g_{m1}/C_c$: a relation among sizes that an equation-based sizer can impose directly. A margin around 60 degrees gives a well-damped step; much less rings, much more is slow and wastes power.

## Going deeper

Gray, Hurst, Lewis and Meyer, "Analysis and Design of Analog Integrated Circuits" (5th ed., 2009), chapter 9; Franklin, Powell and Emami-Naeini, "Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems", chapter 6.

label: Comparators: regeneration and offset
lesson:
# Comparators: regeneration and offset

A comparator decides which of two voltages is larger and produces a logic level. It is the decision element of every ADC, and its speed, offset and metastability set converter performance. Modern comparators are clocked latches that use positive feedback; their regeneration time constant and input-referred offset are the two quantities a converter designer and a sizing tool must compute.

## Regeneration by positive feedback

A latch is two cross-coupled inverters reset to a balanced state and then released with a small imbalance $V_0$. Near balance each side is a transconductor driving a capacitance, and the cross-coupling gives $C\,dv/dt = g_m v$, so the imbalance grows exponentially: $v(t) = V_0 e^{t/\tau}$ with $\tau = C/g_m$. The time to reach a logic level $V_{out}$ is $t = \tau \ln(V_{out}/V_0)$. With $C = 20$ fF and $g_m = 400\ \mu$S, $\tau = 50$ ps (femtofarads over microsiemens is nanoseconds); a 1 mV imbalance reaches 0.8 V in $50 \ln 800 = 334$ ps. Each factor of $e$ in input costs only one $\tau$, which is why latches resolve tiny inputs quickly.

## Metastability

If the decision must be ready by time $T$, the latch fails when the initial imbalance is below $V_{min} = V_{out} e^{-T/\tau}$. With $\tau = 20$ ps, $T = 200$ ps and $V_{out} = 1$ V, $V_{min} = e^{-10} = 45\ \mu$V. Inputs closer to the threshold than this leave the output undecided, a metastable state. For a random input distributed over a range much wider than $V_{min}$, the probability of metastability scales as $e^{-T/\tau}$, so doubling the regeneration time squares down the error rate. In ADCs a metastable comparator can produce large code errors (sparkle codes in flash converters, wrong MSBs in SARs), so designers budget enough time constants per decision and sometimes add metastability detection.

## Offset and the preamplifier

Mismatch between the latch devices gives an input-referred offset, often tens of millivolts for small devices. A preamplifier of gain $A_p$ in front divides the latch's offset by $A_p$ when referred to the input, and contributes its own offset. Independent offsets add in variance: $\sigma_{in} = \sqrt{\sigma_{pre}^2 + (\sigma_{latch}/A_p)^2}$. With a 3 mV preamp offset, a 25 mV latch offset and a gain of 10, $\sigma_{in} = \sqrt{9 + 6.25} = 3.9$ mV. The preamp also isolates the input from latch kickback. The cost is power and delay, so converter designers trade preamp gain against offset calibration, which measures and cancels offset digitally instead of with area or power.

## Going deeper

Razavi, "The StrongARM latch" (IEEE Solid-State Circuits Magazine, 2015); Johns and Martin, "Analog Integrated Circuit Design", chapter on comparators.

problems.q: A cross-coupled latch has regeneration time constant $\tau = C/g_m$ with $C = 39$ fF and $g_m = 2000\ \mu$S. It starts from a 9.9 mV imbalance. How long does it take to regenerate to 0.6 V, in picoseconds? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $\tau = 19.5$ ps. The imbalance grows as $e^{t/\tau}$, so $t = \tau\ln(V_{out}/V_{in}) = 19.5 \cdot \ln(60.61) = 80$ ps.

problems.e: $\tau = 43.333$ ps. The imbalance grows as $e^{t/\tau}$, so $t = \tau\ln(V_{out}/V_{in}) = 43.333 \cdot \ln(293.1) = 246.2$ ps.

problems.e: Refer the latch offset to the input by dividing by the preamp gain, $18/16 = 1.125$ mV, then add independent variances: $\sqrt{1.3^2 + 1.125^2} = 1.72$ mV.

label: Mismatch and Pelgrom's law
lesson:
# Mismatch and Pelgrom's law

Two transistors drawn identically side by side are never identical in silicon. Random dopant fluctuation, line-edge roughness and oxide variations give each device its own threshold voltage and current factor. Pelgrom's law says how large these local differences are and how they shrink with area. It sets the area, and therefore the capacitance and power, of every precision analog block, and it is the statistical model behind Monte Carlo mismatch simulation.

## Local mismatch shrinks with area

Random local variation comes from many independent microscopic sources spread over the gate area. Averaging over more of them reduces the variance in inverse proportion to area. Pelgrom's model states $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = A_{VT}/\sqrt{WL}$ for the threshold difference of a pair, with a process constant $A_{VT}$ typically between about 1 and 5 mV$\cdot\mu$m in modern processes. A similar law holds for the current factor, $\sigma(\Delta\beta/\beta) = A_\beta/\sqrt{WL}$. For $A_{VT} = 3$ mV$\cdot\mu$m and a device of $W = 4\ \mu$m by $L = 1\ \mu$m, $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = 3/2 = 1.5$ mV. The original model adds a distance term for long-range gradients, but at the close spacing of matched pairs the area term dominates, and gradients are handled by layout instead.

## Area for a target sigma

Inverting the law gives the area needed for a matching target: $WL = (A_{VT}/\sigma)^2$. For $A_{VT} = 3$ mV$\cdot\mu$m and a target of 0.5 mV, each device needs $36\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2$. The square is the important part: halving sigma quadruples area. Area brings capacitance, which lowers bandwidth or raises the power needed to drive it. This quadratic cost is the fundamental reason precision analog is expensive, and why designers prefer calibration, chopping or auto-zeroing when they need sub-millivolt offsets. A sizing tool must therefore include mismatch in its formulation: an optimizer that minimizes area without an offset constraint will shrink exactly the devices that set the offset.

## Using the statistics

Mismatch is a zero-mean Gaussian random variable for each device pair. A comparator offset spec of 5 mV with $\sigma = 1.5$ mV is a $3.3\sigma$ limit, met by about 99.9% of instances. Specs are written as a multiple of sigma for a yield target, typically 3 sigma for a block that appears once and more for one replicated thousands of times, such as a comparator in a flash ADC or a cell in an in-memory array. Because $\sigma \propto 1/\sqrt{WL}$, a pair's sigma at a new area follows directly: quadrupling the area halves sigma. Simulators implement the model by drawing a random threshold shift for each device with the Pelgrom sigma for its geometry, which is how Monte Carlo mismatch analysis works.

## Going deeper

Pelgrom, Duinmaijer and Welbers, "Matching properties of MOS transistors" (IEEE JSSC, 1989); Kinget, "Device mismatch and tradeoffs in the design of analog circuits" (IEEE JSSC, 2005).

problems.q: A process has Pelgrom coefficient $A_{VT} = 4.7$ mV$\cdot\mu$m. What is the standard deviation of the threshold-voltage difference between two identical devices with $W = 19\ \mu$m and $L = 2\ \mu$m, in mV? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = A_{VT}/\sqrt{WL} = 4.7/\sqrt{38} = 0.76$ mV.

problems.q: A process has Pelgrom coefficient $A_{VT} = 2.8$ mV$\cdot\mu$m. What is the standard deviation of the threshold-voltage difference between two identical devices with $W = 4.5\ \mu$m and $L = 1\ \mu$m, in mV? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = A_{VT}/\sqrt{WL} = 2.8/\sqrt{4.5} = 1.32$ mV.

problems.e: $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = A_{VT}/\sqrt{WL} = 4.9/\sqrt{35.65} = 0.82$ mV.

problems.e: Invert Pelgrom's law: $WL = (A_{VT}/\sigma)^2 = (4.1/2.8)^2 = 2.14\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2$. Halving sigma costs four times the area.

problems.e: Invert Pelgrom's law: $WL = (A_{VT}/\sigma)^2 = (2/1.1)^2 = 3.31\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2$. Halving sigma costs four times the area.

problems.e: Invert Pelgrom's law: $WL = (A_{VT}/\sigma)^2 = (1.1/2.2)^2 = 0.25\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2$. Halving sigma costs four times the area.

problems.q: A matched pair shows $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = 1.1$ mV. Both devices' gate areas are multiplied by 2, keeping the same shape. What is the new sigma, in mV? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Sigma scales as $1/\sqrt{WL}$, so it changes by a factor $\sqrt{2} = 1.414$: the new value is 0.778 mV.

problems.q: A matched pair shows $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = 1.4$ mV. Both devices' gate areas are multiplied by 2, keeping the same shape. What is the new sigma, in mV? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Sigma scales as $1/\sqrt{WL}$, so it changes by a factor $\sqrt{2} = 1.414$: the new value is 0.99 mV.

label: Offset and current-mismatch budgets
lesson:
# Offset and current-mismatch budgets

Pelgrom's law gives the mismatch of one pair. A circuit's offset or current error combines the mismatch of several pairs, each weighted by how strongly it affects the output. Building that budget tells a designer which devices to enlarge and tells a sizing tool which constraint to impose on which device. The weighting factors turn out to be ratios of transconductances, so gm/Id choices directly shape mismatch.

## Current mismatch in a mirror

A threshold difference $\Delta V_T$ between mirror devices acts like an error on the shared gate voltage. The resulting relative current error is $\Delta I/I = (g_m/I_D)\Delta V_T$. A mirror at $g_m/I_D = 10\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ with $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = 2$ mV has $\sigma(\Delta I/I) = 2\%$; at $g_m/I_D = 5$ it would be 1%. So current mirrors and current sources prefer low $g_m/I_D$ (strong inversion): their threshold mismatch converts into less current error. Input pairs prefer the opposite, high $g_m/I_D$, because for them what matters is the input-referred voltage, not the current. One device-level choice therefore has opposite best values depending on the device's role.

## Adding independent contributions

Threshold and current-factor mismatch are independent, so their contributions add in variance: $\sigma^2(\Delta I/I) = (g_m/I_D)^2\sigma^2(\Delta V_T) + \sigma^2(\Delta\beta/\beta)$. With a 2% threshold term and a 0.5% current-factor term, the total is $\sqrt{4 + 0.25} = 2.06\%$. In strong inversion with large overdrive the current-factor term can dominate; in weak inversion the threshold term always does. The same root-sum-square rule applies to any set of independent error sources, and it is why a budget is written as a table of variances: the largest term is where area or redesign pays off, while shrinking a small term changes almost nothing.

## Input-referred offset of an OTA

In a five-transistor OTA, input-pair mismatch appears directly at the input. Mismatch in the mirror load produces a current error $g_{m3}\Delta V_{T3}$, which the input pair must cancel with a voltage $\Delta V_{T3}\,g_{m3}/g_{m1}$. So $\sigma^2(V_{os}) = \sigma^2(\Delta V_{T1}) + (g_{m3}/g_{m1})^2\sigma^2(\Delta V_{T3})$. With 1.5 mV for each pair and $g_{m3}/g_{m1} = 0.5$, $\sigma(V_{os}) = \sqrt{2.25 + 0.5625} = 1.68$ mV. The design lesson: make the load's $g_m$ small relative to the input pair's, by running the load at lower $g_m/I_D$. An equation-based sizer can impose this budget as a constraint and size each pair's area from Pelgrom's law.

## Going deeper

Kinget, "Device mismatch and tradeoffs in the design of analog circuits" (IEEE JSSC, 2005); Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2017), chapter 19.

label: Common-centroid layout
lesson:
# Common-centroid layout

Random mismatch shrinks with area, but systematic mismatch from gradients across the die does not. Oxide thickness, doping, stress and temperature vary smoothly with position, so two devices placed side by side see slightly different parameters. Common-centroid layout splits each device into unit cells arranged so that every device has the same centroid, which cancels any linear gradient. Checking and generating such patterns is a core task of analog layout tools.

## Centroids of split devices

Split device A into $n$ equal unit cells at positions $(x_i, y_i)$. Under a parameter that varies linearly with position, $p(x, y) = p_0 + g_x x + g_y y$, the device's average parameter is $p_0 + g_x\bar{x} + g_y\bar{y}$, where $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ is the mean position of its cells: its centroid. In a two-row array with row 1 "ABBA" and row 2 "BAAB", A's cells sit at columns 1, 4 (row 1) and 2, 3 (row 2), so its column centroid is $(1+4+2+3)/4 = 2.5$; its row centroid is 1.5. Computing a centroid is averaging coordinates, and it is the quantity that decides how a device responds to any linear gradient.

## Checking a pattern

A pattern is common-centroid when all matched devices share one centroid. Then any linear gradient shifts them equally and the mismatch cancels. For two devices compute both centroids and their distance; zero means common-centroid. "ABBA / BAAB" is: both centroids are (2.5, 1.5). "ABAB / ABAB" is not: A sits at columns 1 and 3, B at 2 and 4, a separation of one pitch, so a gradient of $g$ per pitch creates a mismatch of $g$. A sufficient construction is point symmetry: if rotating the array 180 degrees about its centre maps every A cell to an A cell, A's centroid is the centre, and likewise for B. Layout generators build patterns this way and verifiers check them by computing centroids, which is linear in the number of cells.

## What else matching needs

Common centroid cancels linear gradients only; it is one of several matching principles. Dispersion spreads each device's cells across the array so that higher-order gradients average out. Equal surroundings matter: a cell at the array edge sees different etching and stress than an interior cell, so dummy cells are added around the array. Devices should share orientation, since mobility depends on current direction relative to the crystal, and the routing to each device should be symmetric so that parasitic resistance does not reintroduce mismatch. Each principle costs area and wiring. A layout tool must trade them against each other, which is why matching constraints are expressed explicitly, for example "these four devices common-centroid with dummies", rather than inferred from wirelength.

## Going deeper

Hastings, "The Art of Analog Layout" (2nd ed., 2005), chapters on device matching.

label: Interdigitated layout and gradient cancellation
lesson:
# Interdigitated layout and gradient cancellation

When matched devices must sit in a single row, as fingers of multi-finger transistors usually do, the layout choice is the order of fingers. Interdigitation alternates the devices; mirrored patterns such as ABBA make the order symmetric. Which patterns cancel which gradients is a small computation on finger positions, and it is exactly what a primitive generator in an analog layout tool must get right.

## Finger positions and centroids in one row

Number the fingers along the row and measure each finger's position from the row centre, so a row of $n$ fingers has positions $-(n-1)/2, \dots, (n-1)/2$. A device's centroid is the mean position of its fingers. For "AABB" the positions are $-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5$: A's centroid is -1, B's is $+1$, a separation of 2 pitches. For "ABAB", A sits at -1.5 and 0.5, centroid -0.5; B at $+0.5$; separation 1. For "ABBA", A at $\pm 1.5$ and B at $\pm 0.5$: both centroids are 0. Plain interdigitation halves the separation of the side-by-side layout, and the mirrored pattern removes it. Dummy fingers at both ends do not change centroids; they equalize the surroundings of the outer fingers.

## Linear gradients

Under a linear gradient of $g$ millivolts per pitch along the row, each finger's threshold shifts by $g$ times its position, and a device's mean shift is $g$ times its centroid. The systematic mismatch between A and B is therefore $g\,|\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B|$. With $g = 0.4$ mV per pitch, "AABB" gives 0.8 mV, "ABAB" gives 0.4 mV, and "ABBA" gives zero. Compare this with random mismatch of perhaps 1 mV for the same devices: an unlucky order can create a systematic error as large as the random one, and unlike random mismatch it does not shrink with area. The calculation is cheap enough that a placer can evaluate it inside its inner loop for every candidate order.

## Higher-order gradients

Real gradients are not perfectly linear. A quadratic component $c\,x^2$, for example from stress near a well edge or a hot spot centred on the array, shifts each device by $c$ times the mean of $x^2$ over its fingers. In "ABBA", A's fingers at $\pm 1.5$ give mean $x^2 = 2.25$ and B's at $\pm 0.5$ give 0.25, so with $c = 0.1$ mV per pitch squared the mismatch is 0.2 mV, even though the linear term cancels. Patterns such as "ABBAABBA" or "ABABBABA" spread both devices more evenly and reduce this. The general lesson for a tool designer: a matching pattern is characterized by which moments of the position distribution it equalizes, and a generator should choose the pattern by the gradients it must cancel, not by habit.

## Going deeper

Hastings, "The Art of Analog Layout" (2nd ed., 2005), chapters on device matching.

label: Layout parasitics and post-layout performance
lesson:
# Layout parasitics and post-layout performance

A schematic that meets every spec can fail once it is laid out. Wires add capacitance and resistance, junctions add capacitance, and adjacent routes couple. Extraction turns these into a post-layout netlist, and re-simulation shows the damage. For a tool designer, parasitics are where layout and sizing meet: a router needs constraints derived from circuit sensitivity, and a sizer needs margins for what layout will add.

## Parasitics move poles

Every node's pole is set by its resistance and capacitance, so extra capacitance moves poles down. In a two-stage op-amp the non-dominant pole is $g_{m6}/(2\pi C_{out})$. If the schematic load is 2 pF and the output route adds 0.5 pF, the pole falls by a factor $2/2.5$: from 159 MHz to 127 MHz for $g_{m6} = 2$ mS. Internal high-impedance nodes are even more sensitive, because their schematic capacitance is small, so a few femtofarads of wiring is a large relative change. Extraction tools (Magic in the open flow, and commercial RC extractors) report these capacitances per net, and the designer or a tool compares pre- and post-layout pole positions to find the nets that matter.

## Phase margin after layout

Lower non-dominant poles erode phase margin. With a dominant pole contributing -90 degrees, $\mathrm{PM} = 90 - \arctan(\mathrm{GBW}/f_{p2})$. Take GBW = 50 MHz and $f_{p2} = 159$ MHz in the schematic: PM = 72.5 degrees. After layout, $f_{p2} = 127$ MHz gives 68.5 degrees, a loss of 4 degrees from half a picofarad. Parasitic resistance in series with compensation capacitors or in supply lines adds further shifts, and coupling capacitance between input and output routes can create feedback paths of its own. This is why analog signoff is a post-layout simulation across corners, not a DRC and LVS check, and why phase margin specs carry a margin for layout.

## From sensitivity to routing constraints

The useful output of post-layout analysis is a constraint the router can obey. Suppose the margin must stay at least 60 degrees with GBW = 50 MHz. Then $f_{p2} \ge 50/\tan 30 = 86.6$ MHz, so $C_{out} \le g_{m6}/(2\pi \cdot 86.6\ \mathrm{MHz})$, which is 3.68 pF for $g_{m6} = 2$ mS. With 2 pF of device load, 1.68 pF is left for wiring; at 0.2 fF per micrometre that is a maximum route length of 8400 micrometres. A constraint-driven flow derives such limits from circuit sensitivities, hands them to placement and routing as net-length or capacitance bounds, and re-verifies after extraction. That loop of sensitivity, constraint, layout and verification is the backbone of parasitic-aware analog layout automation.

## Going deeper

Hastings, "The Art of Analog Layout" (2nd ed., 2005); the Magic VLSI layout tool documentation on extraction.

label: Analog layout automation: MAGICAL and ALIGN
lesson:
# Analog layout automation: MAGICAL and ALIGN

Analog layout is still largely hand-drawn, but research and open-source flows now generate layouts from netlists. MAGICAL and ALIGN are the best-known open efforts: both extract analog constraints, place devices under symmetry and matching constraints, route with analog-aware rules and output GDS that is checked by DRC, LVS and post-layout simulation. Their structure shows what an analog layout engine must contain.

## Constraint extraction

A netlist carries no layout intent, so the first stage recognizes structures and emits constraints. Differential pairs (shared source, complementary gates, equal sizes) become symmetry pairs about a common axis. Current mirrors become matched groups, often common-centroid. Sensitive nets such as inputs and high-impedance nodes are marked for short, shielded, symmetric routing. Recognition is pattern matching on the device-net graph, by subgraph rules, graph similarity or learned classifiers. Over-constraining is costly (every match costs area and flexibility) and under-constraining loses performance, so designer annotations are usually allowed to override or add constraints. The constraint set is the interface between circuit knowledge and geometric optimization.

## Placement under symmetry

Placement minimizes area and wirelength subject to non-overlap and the extracted constraints. Mirror symmetry about a vertical axis $x = a$ requires paired devices to satisfy $y_1 = y_2$ and $x_1 + x_2 = 2a$, and self-symmetric devices to be centred on the axis. Two families of placers exist. Topological placers search sequence-pair or B*-tree encodings with simulated annealing; every encoding decodes to a non-overlapping placement, and symmetric-feasible encodings guarantee symmetry. Analytical placers, as in MAGICAL, solve a smooth wirelength and density objective with symmetry as equality constraints or penalties, then legalize. ALIGN builds matched primitives (mirrors, pairs) with parameterized generators first, so the placer handles fewer, larger, already-matched blocks.

## Routing and the verification loop

Analog routing honours symmetric net pairs (mirror-image routes with equal lengths, layers and vias), shielding for sensitive nets, wide wires for current-carrying nets and limits on coupling. The output must pass DRC and LVS, but those prove only legality and connectivity. Acceptance requires extraction and post-layout simulation against the specs. When a spec fails, the flow must trace the failure to parasitics and feed it back as tighter constraints or re-sizing, which is the hardest part to automate. Published results compare generated layouts with manual ones on post-layout performance; for a tool designer the lesson is that an analog layout engine is a loop around constraints and simulation, not a one-pass placer and router.

## Going deeper

Xu et al., "MAGICAL: Toward fully automated analog IC layout leveraging human and machine intelligence" (ICCAD, 2019); Kunal et al., "ALIGN: Open-source analog layout automation from the ground up" (DAC, 2019).

C) Find which extracted parasitics moved the poles and feed that back as constraints (shorter routes, lower-capacitance layers) or as re-sizing

D) Declare the layout correct since LVS passed

problems.e: Closing the loop means turning extracted sensitivity into constraints or sizing changes; random re-runs rarely fix a systematic parasitic.

A generated layout passes DRC and LVS. Which check is still needed before it is accepted?

A) A second DRC run with tighter rules

B) Post-layout simulation of the extracted netlist against the specs

C) Static timing analysis

D) None, DRC and LVS prove performance
problems.a: Post-layout simulation of the extracted netlist against the specs
problems.e: DRC and LVS prove manufacturability and connectivity, not performance. Only simulation with parasitics shows whether specs still hold.

label: Analog sizing as optimization
lesson:
# Analog sizing as optimization

Sizing chooses device dimensions, bias currents and passive values for a fixed topology so that every specification holds. Written as mathematics it is a constrained, usually multi-objective, nonconvex optimization problem whose functions are evaluated by simulation. Every automated sizer, from geometric programming to Bayesian optimization to an agent, is a choice of how to pose and solve this problem, so the formulation comes first.

## Variables, objective and constraints

The decision variables are widths, lengths (or $g_m/I_D$ and $L$ per device), bias currents, and capacitor and resistor values: perhaps 10 to 50 continuous numbers for an op-amp. Specifications become constraints on simulated performances: gain at least 70 dB, GBW at least 50 MHz, phase margin at least 60 degrees, noise, offset, swing. One or two quantities that should be as small as possible, typically power and area, become the objective. Operating-point constraints keep every device in its intended region with margin, so small-signal specs remain meaningful. Writing a spec as an objective ("maximize GBW") is a common mistake: it spends power beyond what the system needs. A spec with a threshold is a constraint.

## Choosing among candidates

Given simulated candidates, the formulation decides which one wins. First discard every candidate that violates any constraint; then rank the rest by the objective. A candidate with the lowest power overall is worthless if it misses GBW by 1 MHz. When constraints are hard to satisfy, optimizers often work with a penalty: minimize the objective plus a weighted sum of normalized violations $\max(0, (\mathrm{spec} - \mathrm{measured})/\mathrm{spec})$. Normalization makes specs in different units comparable. A penalty method can return a slightly infeasible point with a better objective, so a careful flow re-checks feasibility exactly and treats any remaining violation as failure.

## Robustness, trade-offs and solution methods

A design that meets specs at the typical corner and fails at the slow corner is not a solution, so robust formulations constrain the worst case over corners or a yield target under Monte Carlo. With two objectives, such as power and GBW, the answer is a Pareto front of non-dominated designs, which lets the system designer choose the trade-off knowingly. Solution methods split by how they evaluate performance. Equation-based methods use analytical or fitted models, sometimes posynomials for geometric programming, which is convex and solves to global optimality in seconds, but only for the model. Simulation-based methods treat SPICE as a black box and search with evolutionary algorithms, simulated annealing or Bayesian optimization, which are accurate but limited by the simulation budget.

## Going deeper

Gielen and Rutenbar, "Computer-aided design of analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 2000); del Mar Hershenson, Boyd and Lee, "Optimal design of a CMOS op-amp via geometric programming" (IEEE TCAD, 2001).

label: Equation-based sizing
lesson:
# Equation-based sizing

Equation-based sizing writes each performance as an explicit function of the design variables and solves the resulting system or optimization directly. In its simplest form it is the designer's hand procedure scripted: start from GBW and load, derive transconductances, then currents and widths. In its most formal form, posynomial models make the problem a geometric program. Its speed makes it the natural inner model for exploration and a starting point for simulation-based refinement.

## From GBW to the input pair

In a Miller two-stage op-amp, $\mathrm{GBW} = g_{m1}/(2\pi C_c)$. Choosing $C_c$ (often a fraction of the load capacitance, for stability and noise) fixes the input-pair transconductance: $g_{m1} = 2\pi \cdot \mathrm{GBW} \cdot C_c$. For GBW = 40 MHz and $C_c = 2$ pF, $g_{m1} = 2\pi \cdot 40 \cdot 2 = 502.7\ \mu$S, using the unit identity that MHz times pF gives microsiemens. The procedure works backwards from specs to device parameters, and each step uses an equation that is exact within its model. A sizing script can evaluate the whole chain in microseconds, so it can sweep $C_c$ or other free choices to explore the space before any simulation.

## From transconductance to current and size

With $g_{m1}$ known, the gm/Id methodology gives the bias. Choosing $g_m/I_D = 15\ \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ for the input pair (high efficiency and low noise, at the cost of linear range) gives $I_D = 502.7/15 = 33.5\ \mu$A per side and a tail current of 67 microamperes. The width follows from the lookup table's current density at that $g_m/I_D$ and the chosen $L$. Each device is sized the same way from its own role: mirror loads at low $g_m/I_D$ for matching, the second-stage driver from the stability condition below. Because every quantity comes from a model, the procedure is only as accurate as its device data, which is why lookup tables replaced square-law equations in modern equation-based flows.

## Stability as a sizing equation

Phase margin becomes an equation by placing the non-dominant pole: require $g_{m6}/(2\pi C_L) \ge k\cdot\mathrm{GBW}$ with $k$ around 2.2 for roughly 65 degrees. For GBW = 40 MHz and $C_L = 5$ pF, $g_{m6} \ge 2.2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 40 \cdot 5 = 2765\ \mu$S. Note the asymmetry: the second stage needs several times the input pair's transconductance, so it dominates power. Equation-based optimizers collect such relations (gain, poles, slew, swing, noise) and either solve them in sequence, as above, or hand them to a solver. Geometric programming fits each performance as a posynomial in the variables, which makes the problem convex after a log change of variables, so the global optimum of the model is found reliably. The weakness is model error: short-channel devices are not posynomial, so the result must be verified, and usually refined, in SPICE.

## Going deeper

del Mar Hershenson, Boyd and Lee, "Optimal design of a CMOS op-amp via geometric programming" (IEEE TCAD, 2001); Jespers and Murmann, "Systematic Design of Analog CMOS Circuits Using Pre-Computed Lookup Tables" (2017).
